_comment: Editorial introductions rendered at the top of each document partial. Edit freely; re-run `node scripts/build-faith-received.mjs` to regenerate the partials. Voice: brief, scholarly, pastorally serious. No em dashes (use a regular dash with spaces).
polanus-syntagma: Amandus Polanus von Polansdorf (1561-1610) wrote the Syntagma Theologiae Christianae as a working textbook for the Reformed academy at Basel; the first folio appeared in 1609, the definitive Hanau edition in 1615. It is the first fully systematic Reformed scholastic theology, organised on the bifurcating Ramist method: every locus is divided into two, then two again, until the entire matter of dogmatics has been distributed across ten books. Wollebius, Maccovius, Gomarus and the wider Dutch Reformed tradition all leaned on it. This English edition is Stiven Peter's translation of the SCTA diplomatic transcription of the 1615 Hanau folio, paired with a facing Latin-English verification edition and released, like the source, under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. As of this edition only Liber I (De Theologiae Principiis - on the principles of theology) is available; the remaining nine books will be added as the translation progresses.
apostles-creed: The Apostles' Creed is the earliest and most concise statement of the Christian faith - a baptismal confession that took shape over the second through fourth centuries as the Church taught new converts what to believe and what to renounce. It carries the structure of a triune confession: the Father who creates, the Son who redeems, the Spirit who sustains. To recite it is to enter the long company of Christians who have answered the question, "What do you believe?" with these same words.
nicene-creed: The Nicene Creed was hammered out at the councils of Nicaea in 325 and Constantinople in 381 to answer the most pressing question of the early Church: who exactly is Jesus of Nazareth? Against Arius, who taught that the Son was a creature, the Council confessed the Son as homoousios - of the same substance as the Father, true God from true God. The Creed remains the most widely received doctrinal standard in Christendom, recited by Catholic, Orthodox, and most Protestant churches alike.
chalcedonian: At the Council of Chalcedon in 451, the Church faced its second great Christological crisis: not whether the Son was fully God, but how he could be both fully God and fully human in one person. The Chalcedonian Definition gives the answer in four adverbs - without confusion, without change, without division, without separation. Christ is one and the same, made known in two natures. This is the language Christianity has used ever since to confess the Incarnation.
athanasian: The Athanasian Creed, despite its name, was not written by Athanasius but emerged from the Latin West sometime between the fifth and sixth centuries. It is the longest and most thorough of the ecumenical creeds, repeating its central confession with the precision of a song so it cannot be misheard: the Trinity in Unity, the Unity in Trinity. Its sharp anathemas - "this is the catholic faith, which except a man believe faithfully, he cannot be saved" - were meant to be read aloud in worship.
didache: The Didache, or "Teaching of the Twelve Apostles," is the earliest surviving Christian church order outside the New Testament - written sometime between the late first and early second century. It is a manual: how to live the Way of Life, how to be baptized, how to celebrate the Eucharist, how to recognize true and false teachers. To read it is to overhear the Church's earliest pastoral instincts, the Way of Life and the Way of Death set side by side without commentary.
diognetus: The Letter to Diognetus is a second- or third-century Christian apology to a pagan inquirer, asking why Christians live as they do. The author - unknown to us - answers with one of the most striking descriptions of the Christian's place in the world ever written: Christians dwell in the world as the soul dwells in the body, holding it together precisely because they love it without belonging to it. The letter is often anthologized as a foundational document of Christian political theology.
augsburg: The Augsburg Confession, presented to Emperor Charles V in 1530 by the Lutheran electors, is the founding doctrinal document of the Protestant Reformation. Drafted by Philip Melanchthon under Luther's review, it sets out the Reformation's case in 28 articles: justification by faith, the authority of Scripture, the right administration of the sacraments. The Confession was a peace offering as much as a manifesto, hoping the Roman party would recognize Lutheran teaching as an internal reform of the catholic Church.
belgic: The Belgic Confession was written in 1561 by Guido de Brès, a Reformed pastor preaching in the Spanish-occupied Low Countries. He composed it under threat of execution, hoping to persuade the Catholic authorities that the Reformed faith was not sedition but the catholic Christian faith. The Confession was thrown over the wall of the King of Spain's castle at Tournai shortly after it was written. Two years later, de Brès was hanged for it.
thirty-nine-articles: The Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion were finalized in 1571 to define the doctrinal position of the Church of England between the Roman and Reformed extremes after the upheaval of the English Reformation. They are deliberately moderate and broadly Protestant - Reformed in their doctrine of grace, churchly in their sacramental theology, open enough to hold together a national church. They remain the doctrinal standard of the Anglican Communion.
1689: The Second London Baptist Confession, often called the 1689, is the most thorough confession of the Reformed Baptist tradition. Its English drafters worked closely from the Westminster Confession, copying Westminster's language wherever they agreed and rewriting only on baptism, the church, and civil government. The result is a document that sits inside the Reformed family while staking out a particular polity: believer's baptism, congregational church order, religious liberty under the civil magistrate.
heidelberg: The Heidelberg Catechism was written in 1563 for the churches of the Palatinate by Zacharias Ursinus and Caspar Olevianus, on commission from the elector Frederick III. It asks the reader a single, enormous question: "What is your only comfort, in life and in death?" The 128 questions that follow are an exposition of that answer - a map of the Christian life from misery through deliverance into gratitude, organized into 52 Lord's Days for weekly preaching. Four and a half centuries later, it remains one of the warmest and most pastoral documents the Reformation produced.
westminster-shorter: The Westminster Shorter Catechism was finalized in 1647 by the Westminster Assembly, an English parliamentary body convened to bring the worship and doctrine of the Church of England into conformity with Reformed practice. Its 107 questions and answers were written for children and new converts, but its precision is such that adults still find it the surest summary of Reformed doctrine in English. It opens with one of the most-quoted lines in Protestant history: man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him forever.
westminster-larger: The Westminster Larger Catechism, finalized alongside the Shorter in 1647, was written for the pulpit rather than the home - an exposition of the same doctrine in 196 questions, with longer answers, fuller scripture proofs, and more careful distinctions. Where the Shorter Catechism gives a definition, the Larger walks through implications. Where the Shorter answers in a sentence, the Larger answers in a paragraph. Together they remain the standards of the Reformed Presbyterian tradition.
lausanne: The Lausanne Covenant was issued by the 1974 International Congress on World Evangelization, convened in Lausanne by Billy Graham and John Stott. Its 15 articles are the founding statement of contemporary global evangelicalism - a confession of biblical authority, a call to evangelism inseparable from social concern, and an explicit repentance for the cultural captivity of Western missions. It remains the closest thing modern evangelical Protestantism has to an ecumenical creed.
ninety-five-theses: On October 31, 1517, Martin Luther - then an Augustinian monk and professor at Wittenberg - posted 95 propositions challenging the sale of indulgences. He intended a scholarly disputation; he ignited the Protestant Reformation. The Theses themselves are not yet the mature Lutheran Reformation: they are a young theologian's pastoral protest against a particular abuse, working out the deeper logic of repentance and the gospel as he writes.
edwards-resolutions: Jonathan Edwards composed his Resolutions between 1722 and 1723, while he was in his late teens and early twenties. They are private - meant to be re-read once a week, "remembering," as he put it, "to be sensible that I am unable to do anything without God's help." They give us a window into the most rigorous Reformed mind New England ever produced as that mind was forming itself: terrifyingly disciplined, candidly self-aware, oriented entirely toward the glory of God.
athanasius-incarnation: Athanasius wrote On the Incarnation around 318, before the Council of Nicaea, before he was made Bishop of Alexandria, before the long years of exile. It is his classic defense of why God became man - to undo death, restore the image, and conquer the corruption introduced into the human race by sin. C.S. Lewis, who wrote the introduction to the standard English translation, called it "a masterpiece" by "a great theologian."
augustine-confessions: Augustine wrote the Confessions in his early forties, between 397 and 400, a decade after his conversion. They are the first great Western autobiography - an extended meditation on memory, time, sin, grace, and the restless heart that finds no rest until it rests in God. The book is addressed entirely to God in the second person; the reader is overhearing a conversation between a great soul and his Maker.
calvin-institutes: John Calvin published the first edition of the Institutes of the Christian Religion in 1536, when he was 26, as a small handbook for French Protestants suffering under persecution. He revised and expanded it for the rest of his life; the final 1559 edition, from which the standard modern texts descend, is the foundational systematic theology of the Reformed tradition. Calvin's structure follows the Apostles' Creed: God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, and the means of grace.
charnock-attributes: Stephen Charnock, an English Puritan ejected from his Anglican living in 1662, spent the last decades of his life preaching what would become the great work of his career. Published posthumously in 1682, The Existence and Attributes of God is the most thorough Puritan treatment of the divine perfections in the English language - fourteen discourses on God's existence, eternity, immutability, omnipresence, knowledge, wisdom, power, holiness, goodness, dominion, and patience. The work is intellectually demanding and pastorally devastating in equal measure.
imitation-of-christ: The Imitation of Christ, written in Latin between 1418 and 1427 and traditionally attributed to Thomas à Kempis of the Brethren of the Common Life, is the most widely read Christian devotional work after the Bible. It is a guide to the interior life - the cultivation of humility, the renunciation of self, the love of God in solitude - drawn from the Devotio Moderna tradition of late-medieval Holland. Read by Catholics and Protestants alike for six centuries, it remains a sober warning against every form of religion that does not change the heart.
rerum-novarum: Pope Leo XIII published Rerum Novarum on May 15, 1891, addressing what the title calls "new things" - the upheavals of the industrial revolution, the rise of socialism, and the condition of the working classes. The encyclical condemns both Marxist collectivism and laissez-faire capitalism, defends the right to private property, the dignity of labor, and the just wage, and is the foundational text of modern Catholic Social Teaching. Its influence on Christian social and political thought across the twentieth century is difficult to overstate.
1928-bcp: The 1928 Book of Common Prayer is the last revision of the American Prayer Book before the controversial 1979 edition that replaced it. It contains the full liturgical life of the Anglican Church: the Daily Office of Morning and Evening Prayer, the Holy Communion, the sacramental rites of Baptism, Confirmation, Matrimony, and the Visitation of the Sick, the Burial of the Dead, the Ordinal for making deacons, priests, and bishops, the Psalter in Coverdale's translation arranged for the 30-day cycle, and the prayers and thanksgivings that mark the occasions of ordinary life. The daily office preserves the structure Cranmer laid down in 1549. This edition presents the original Elizabethan English alongside a modernized reading for those who prefer contemporary language, while preserving the cadence and theology of the text.
